prior_art_found: MIT / Alex Kachkine generative-AI painting-restoration method (Nature, June 2025): reconstructs losses with generative AI, builds an exact-colour retouch MAP confined to losses, applies a removable/reversible film with conservation varnish, stores the digital mask for future conservators — matches the candidate's masked-fill + edit-map + reversibility + conservator-decision-aid framing essentially 1:1.

'Machine learning for painting conservation: a state-of-the-art review' (npj Heritage Science, 2025) — names 'virtual restoration' (incl. lacuna inpainting) as an established ML theme, refuting the very-low-penetration premise.
Generative-AI digital restoration of Callet's 'Achilles' (AccScience, 2024) — explicitly positions generative inpainting as guidance for conservators before physical restoration.

ICCV 2025 Workshop 'Visual Design from Cultural Heritage through Inpainting-based Restoration'; DiffuMural / GuidePaint diffusion mural inpainting (npj Heritage Science 2025); Nature Scientific Reports 2026 deep-generative artifact inpainting; 'Assisting classical paintings restoration: paint loss detection + descriptor-based inpainting'; Colour-Balanced Edge-Guided Digital Inpainting on artworks.
Earlier DL art-restoration pipelines (DDCNN, arXiv 2023; dual-attention/channel-transformer GAN for damaged artwork).
verdict_reason: The application already exists in directly equivalent form. The candidate frames a generative, mask-constrained, context-conditioned fill that paints ONLY documented losses, is reversible, matches surrounding palette/varnish, and serves as a conservator decision-support visualization with explicit edit maps before physical retouch. The MIT/Kachkine method (Nature 2025) realizes every one of these elements (generative reconstruction -> exact-colour retouch map over losses only -> reversible varnish-adhered film -> stored mask for documentation), and a 2025 npj Heritage Science review plus ICCV 2025 and multiple Nature diffusion-inpainting heritage papers show masked generative loss-filling for paintings is an established, even productized, area. Swapping the specific generative backbone to InternVL-U (a months-old unified model) does not constitute a first application: the technique class (masked generative fill respecting surrounding context, used as conservator decision support for reversible physical loss-filling) is already deployed. As flagged in the task, candidate 4's gap is closed.

NO prior art found for the specific pairing: a multivariate time-series FOUNDATION model (Toto / zero-few-shot cross-channel) applied to in-tank soy-sauce or miso moromi telemetry to forecast the maturity-ready window.
verdict_reason: Some ML/AI work clearly exists on this exact domain problem: E-nose/PTR-TOF-MS + ML already predicts soy-sauce fermentation stage, NIR+chemometrics monitors moromi in real time, ML estimates maturity-correlated indices, and — notably — the candidate's own cited source already provides an objective moromi-maturity method (SEM+PCAS). Generic multivariate time-series deep-learning forecasting of fermentation from sensor probes (LSTM, etc.) is also established. So the 'no objective method / very-low-AI-penetration' premise is overstated and the broad problem is touched. However, the SPECIFIC technique and framing the candidate proposes — a pretrained multivariate time-series FOUNDATION model (Toto 2.0) doing zero/few-shot, cross-channel forecasting of in-tank fermentation telemetry to project the convergence/ready-window for soy-sauce or miso moromi — returns no prior art: existing soy-sauce ML is stage classification or point quality estimation (not trajectory forecasting), and existing TS-forecasting deep learning is on other fermentation substrates with bespoke (non-foundation) models. The gap is therefore narrowed but not closed: the foundation-model-forecasting-of-moromi-maturity formulation is genuinely new, while the underlying objective-maturity goal is no longer virgin territory.
